zh.question: 头顶的星光怎样连到银河、太阳系和地球，再连到更大的宇宙？
zh.observe: 沿四条主线探索：先从地面夜空、命名恒星的远近到银河全貌，再同尺对照其他星系；向内保留地球的物理定位，从银河经过恒星邻域与太阳系，靠近地月系统和地球；其他恒星家庭在独立对照镜头中观察，不表示它们彼此相邻。向外区分银河、本星系群、邻近星系团、超星系团、宇宙网与可观测范围。最后用地球到宇宙的一次连续拉远串起这些尺度。天体直径、太阳近景和星团作为可选细看，不再与四条主线竞争。先按短提示操作，再打开当前画面的解说。

academic.title: 同一长度单位跨越多个量级
academic.body: 模型始终以 km 保存距离，滑杆控制视野宽度的对数而不是把每个天体的半径分别取对数。同一帧内的几何投影保持线性。km、AU 和光年是不同大小的长度单位；超小天体转换为定位符，定位符与真实直径明确分开。大犬座 VY 使用 2012 年约 1420 个太阳半径的光球估计；St2-18 由 2012 年光度与温度推得约 2150 个太阳半径，依赖不确定的距离与星团归属。它们是估计案例，不是最大恒星排行榜。 TRAPPIST-1轨道与水星轨道使用共同线性AU尺；近景只改变取景范围。七颗行星共享演示天数和选定轨道周期，圆轨道、相位、放大定位球和假想表面不代表完整多体计算或观测地图。 完整行星阵容的展开布局不作距离比较；太阳系各行星周期由既有AU轨道半径按圆轨道开普勒近似计算。 向内镜头反向使用同一物理映射，地月距离与两者半径不分别放大。Kepler-16采用所选2011年椭圆轨道参数和约41.08天、228.78天周期；天鹅座X-1采用约5.60天近圆双星参考，两者都不是完整多体或气体动力学求解。

academic.title: 银河系的空间结构
academic.body: 银河系是棒旋星系，包括扁平恒星盘、中央核球与棒、较稀疏恒星晕和气体等成分。太阳位于盘内，距中心约二万六千光年；本场景取盘半径约五万光年作结构参照。改变视角只改变投影，不重新分布恒星：正面便于找旋臂，侧面便于比较盘与晕的厚度。旋涡、椭圆和不规则是形态案例，不是所有星系必经的演化序列。星团是恒星集合，能作为星系的组成部分；星系群的成员则是多座星系。不能靠亮点数量或圆不圆作统一分类。暗物质晕由引力效应间接推断；本章的可见星点晕只代表恒星晕。中心黑洞主导邻近区域，并不把整个银河变成巨大的太阳系。 银河光带来自盘内观察；不同视线穿过的星光和尘埃不同。星座是天空区域与投影图案，不是物理层级中的一座星系。猎户座七颗亮星使用J2000方向和2007年Hipparcos视差倒数示例；亮星和多星的距离有研究差异，误差条只对应视差形式误差，不含所有系统误差。部分恒星可能同属星协，认星连线本身不证明物理连接。M31与M87为真实对象案例，三维点群仍是结构重建示意。 太阳也是恒星；天空中的亮点可能是恒星、反光的行星或卫星，也可能包含未分开的多星系统。M31具有与银河不同的尘埃与恒星形成环；不规则案例采用巴纳德星系NGC 6822的观测形态参考。星系同尺对照使用所选恒星主体跨度：银河约10万、M31约20万、M87选定明亮主体约12万光年；NGC 6822由0.50 Mpc与16角分长轴推得约7600光年。这些范围不共享统一等亮度边界，不能排序完整星晕或总质量。

academic.title: 地图是有边界的重建
academic.body: 银河系的外观模型根据内部观测重建，而不是从外面拍摄的完整照片。本星系群不仅有银河、仙女座和三角座星系，还包含大、小麦哲伦云等许多矮星系。室女座星系团是另一个邻近结构，不包含本星系群；按拉尼亚凯亚的流向重建，两者都处于这一广大区域，但边界取决于观测和模型，超星系团整体通常不受自身引力束缚。宇宙网是大尺度分布形态，不是容纳拉尼亚凯亚的独立外壳。结构路径图不按比例；可观测范围画面与连续镜头终点共用一套统计示意网，中心定位符并非超星系团直径。远处丝线、结点与小光点不是个别星系的实测位置或大小，不能凭画面测量。最远端的长度表示今天的空间距离量级，不等于光走过的年数；本图不模拟宇宙膨胀或光行回溯时间。

zh.misconception: 光年是距离；太阳系、星团、星系和星系群是不同层次。星系转到侧面不会变成另一种星系；形态类别也不是必然的演化顺序。可观测范围以观察者为参照，不说明地球是宇宙物理中心，视界不是宇宙边墙。 天上的仙女座区域不等于仙女座星系；看起来相邻的恒星不一定同样远。TRAPPIST-1与太阳系同属行星系统，M31与银河系同属星系。 恒星、恒星系统与星系不是同义词；一个光点也不保证只含一颗恒星。Kepler-16是有已确认环双星行星的系统，天鹅座X-1是恒星与黑洞伴星系统，此处不为它添加未经确认的行星。
zh.boundary: 地球表面、星点分布与星系外观为结构插画。所有十字和空心小圈都表示位置，不是被放大的真实尺寸。星系方向为示意，银河晕范围非精确边界，本星系群的小星系点只是抽样，不是成员普查。天体对比只比较直径，不表示质量或实际间隔；大角星采用约 25.4 个太阳半径的估计。结构图不按尺寸和距离比例；连续镜头的大尺度丝线和光点也不能用标尺测量。可观测视界不是整个宇宙的物理边缘。 新增星系观察使用稳定的教学点群与三维空间，点数和亮度不是实测恒星数；单独观察和星团放大图独立取景；「同尺看星系」另采用共同光年换算，主体跨度的定义并不统一。本星系群可旋转图只说明成员归属，位置、尺寸和方向不可量取。正面与侧面使用同一组几何，不计算星系演化或恒星轨道。 夜空新增命名恒星使用目录方向，与原有统计星点明确区分。未命名背景、银河光带强弱与尘埃细节为增强结构投影，非此时此地的完整星图；M31光斑为方向定位而放大。猎户座距离为明确年代的有误差输入，不模拟恒星移动。 地面夜空与空间镜头为独立模式，不把地平线混入空间中的镜头移动。完整行星对照包括中央恒星与主要行星；卫星、小天体与更远处储库不在本次阵容中。星系同尺图不表示真实相邻，不含完整暗物质晕、气体晕与极暗恒星外围。 球状星团的两幅图复用同一组恒星示意，银晕位置与放大定位符不对应某个已命名星团。Kepler-16与天鹅座X-1的轨道使用指定近似与示意相位，定位球放大，行星表面和热气体为插画，不是实拍、流体求解或相对论光线追踪。

narration.label: 从夜空认识银河
narration.text: 先抬头看星光。太阳也是恒星，只是离我们最近。夜空中的许多星点，是银河里很远的恒星；有些亮点则是反光的行星，或者还没有分开的多颗恒星。银河光带混合了许多恒星的光。我们从薄盘里面看它，再换到外面，便知道这条光带来自哪里。银河还有不同模样的邻居；比较大小时，需要同一把长度尺。
narration.cue: 从地面夜空切到沿盘面观察；查看命名恒星的距离，再观察银河全貌和同尺星系对照。

narration.label: 向里找我们的家
narration.text: 现在在银河中找到太阳所在的位置，逐步靠近恒星邻域和太阳系，再找到地球与月球，最后回到地球。旁边的对照镜头里，还可以认识不同的恒星家庭。有的只有一颗中央恒星，有的行星绕着两颗恒星转，也有恒星与黑洞相伴。行星反射恒星光；黑洞附近明亮的气体，不是黑洞自己在发光。
narration.cue: 按向内停靠点靠近地球；单独进入恒星家庭，播放Kepler-16或天鹅座X-1公转，再返回地月视窗。

narration.label: 向外看更大的结构
narration.text: 再从银河向外看。银河和许多其他星系属于本星系群；邻近的室女座星系团，是另一个可以比较的结构。更广大区域的归属，需要观测与模型来研究。宇宙网描述大尺度分布，不是一层发光的外壳。画面尺度变大时，一个定位点可能代表整座星系，所以不能总把每个点都当作一颗恒星。
narration.cue: 依次查看银河、星系群、星系团对照、超星系团、宇宙网与可观测范围；强调成员、邻居与统计示意的区别。

narration.label: 从地球一路拉远
narration.text: 最后，让镜头从地球一路拉远。开始看得到地球的轮廓，后来只能靠定位符找到我们。太阳系、银河和更大的结构逐渐进入画面，长度尺也不断改变。最后的虚线是从这里能观测到的范围参考，不是整个宇宙的一堵墙，也不说明地球是宇宙的中心。
narration.cue: 在第四章播放完整连续拉远，途中停下或回退，对照物理标尺、定位锚点与当前模型限定。

en.question: How do sky lights connect to our galaxy, Solar System and Earth, and then to the wider universe?
en.observe: Follow four routes. Begin with the ground sky and the depths of named stars, reach the whole Milky Way and compare other galaxies on one length ruler. Inward, retain the physical Earth locator from the galaxy through nearby stars and the Solar System to Earth and Moon, then Earth. Other stellar families appear in separate comparison windows, not as neighbours in this journey. Outward, distinguish the Milky Way, Local Group, nearby clusters, superclusters, cosmic web and observable region. Finish with one continuous zoom from Earth. Diameter comparisons, the Sun close-up and star clusters remain optional inspections. Follow the short cue, then open the explanation of the current scene.

academic.title: One length system across many orders of magnitude
academic.body: Distances remain in kilometers. The slider changes the logarithm of view width; it does not separately take logarithms of body radii. Geometry within each frame remains a linear projection. Kilometers, AU and light-years are all length units. Subpixel bodies switch to explicit position symbols rather than silently enlarged disks. VY Canis Majoris uses a 2012 photospheric estimate of about 1420 solar radii. St2-18 uses about 2150 solar radii inferred from 2012 luminosity and temperature values, conditional on uncertain distance and cluster membership. These are estimated examples, not a largest-star ranking. TRAPPIST-1 and Mercury share a linear AU orbital scale; close-up only changes framing. Seven planets share elapsed days and selected periods. Circular orbits, authored phases, enlarged locators and hypothetical surfaces are not a many-body solution or observed maps. The spread whole-system layout is not a distance comparison. Solar planet periods use a circular Kepler approximation from the existing AU orbital radii. The inward camera reverses the same physical mapping; Earth–Moon separation and body radii are not independently enlarged. Kepler-16 uses a selected 2011 elliptical reference with periods about 41.08 and 228.78 days; Cygnus X-1 uses a nearly circular roughly 5.60-day binary reference. Neither is a full many-body or gas-dynamics solution.

academic.title: The structure of the Milky Way
academic.body: The Milky Way is a barred spiral with a flattened stellar disk, central bulge and bar, sparse stellar halo, gas and other components. The Sun lies in the disk about 26,000 light-years from the centre; a rounded 50,000-light-year disk radius provides a structural reference here. Changing the view changes projection rather than reshuffling stars: face-on reveals arms, while edge-on compares disk and halo depth. Spiral, elliptical and irregular are morphological cases, not a compulsory evolutionary sequence. Star clusters are stellar collections that can belong to a galaxy; galaxy groups contain multiple galaxies. Dot counts and roundness do not define a universal classification. Dark matter is inferred from gravity; the visible halo dots in this chapter represent the stellar halo only. The central black hole governs nearby orbits, not the whole galaxy as a giant Solar System. The sky band is an inside-disk view. Constellations are sky regions and projected patterns, not galaxies. Orion uses J2000 directions and selected reciprocal 2007 Hipparcos parallaxes. Bright and multiple-star distances differ between studies; bars show only formal parallax errors. Some stars can share associations; pattern lines alone establish no physical link. M31 and M87 are real examples, while their point volumes remain structural illustrations. The Sun is a star; sky lights may also be reflecting planets or satellites, or unresolved multiple systems. M31 has distinctive dust and star-forming rings. The irregular example uses observations of Barnard’s Galaxy, NGC 6822. A common length conversion uses selected stellar-body spans of about 100,000, 200,000 and 120,000 light-years for the Milky Way, M31 and a bright M87 body; NGC 6822 uses about 7,600 light-years from 0.50 Mpc and a 16-arcminute major axis. These are not uniform-isophote boundaries or rankings of complete halos or total masses.

academic.title: A reconstruction with defined limits
academic.body: The external Milky Way view is reconstructed from observations made inside it, not photographed from outside. Beyond the Milky Way, the Local Group includes Andromeda, Triangulum and many dwarf galaxies such as the Magellanic Clouds. The Virgo Cluster is a separate nearby structure, not a container for the Local Group. In a Laniakea flow reconstruction both occupy the wider region, but its boundary depends on observations and the model, and the supercluster is generally not bound as a whole. The cosmic web is a pattern of large-scale distribution, not a separate shell around Laniakea. Address diagrams are not to scale; the observable-region view and the continuous camera's endpoint share one statistical illustration, and the central locator is not the supercluster's diameter. Distant filaments, knots and points are not measured positions or sizes of individual galaxies and cannot be measured from the picture. The far-end length is an approximate present-day spatial distance, not light-travel time; expansion and lookback time are not simulated.

en.misconception: A light-year is a distance. Solar systems, star clusters, galaxies and galaxy groups are different levels. An edge-on view does not change a galaxy’s category, and morphology is not a compulsory evolutionary sequence. An observer-centred observable region does not make Earth the physical centre of the universe; its horizon is not a wall. The Andromeda sky region is not the Andromeda galaxy. Nearby-looking stars need not be equally distant. TRAPPIST-1 and the Solar System are planetary systems; M31 and the Milky Way are galaxies. A star, a stellar system and a galaxy are different concepts; one unresolved point need not contain one star. Kepler-16 has a confirmed circumbinary planet. Cygnus X-1 is a star–black-hole binary; no unconfirmed planet is added.
en.boundary: Earth’s surface, individual point distribution and external galaxy appearance are illustrations. Crosshairs and tiny open circles show locations, not inflated physical sizes. Directions are schematic, halo limits are not precise boundaries, and the small-galaxy marks are a sample, not a Local Group census. Body comparisons show diameters, not masses or separations; Arcturus uses an estimated 25.4 solar radii. Structure diagrams have no size or distance scale, and filaments and points in the continuous long-range camera cannot be measured with its ruler. The observable horizon is not the physical edge of the whole universe. The galaxy study uses stable teaching populations in 3D, not measured star counts or photometry. Individual inspections and cluster close-ups are framed independently; Galaxies on one ruler instead shares a light-year conversion with differently defined selected body extents. The rotatable Local Group illustration shows membership; its positions, sizes and directions are not measurable. Face-on and edge-on views use the same geometry, without computing galaxy evolution or stellar orbits. Newly named sky stars use catalogue directions, distinct from statistical background points. Diffuse light, dust and unnamed points are enhanced structural projections, not a complete live local sky chart. M31’s directional patch is enlarged. Orion distances are explicitly dated, uncertain inputs, without stellar motion. Ground sky and spatial cameras are separate modes; the horizon does not blend into spatial travel. The whole planetary comparison includes each central star and its major planets, excluding moons, small bodies and more distant reservoirs. The common-scale galaxy diagram is not real adjacency and excludes complete dark-matter halos, gas halos and very faint stellar outskirts. The two cluster views reuse one stellar illustration; its halo location and enlarged locator do not identify a named measured cluster. Kepler-16 and Cygnus X-1 use specified orbit approximations and illustrative phases. Body locators are enlarged; planetary surfaces and hot gas are illustrations, not photographs, fluid solutions or relativistic ray tracing.

narration.label: From sky to galaxies
narration.text: Begin with the sky. The Sun is a star, and it is our nearest one. Many night-sky points are distant Milky Way stars; some lights are reflecting planets, or multiple stars we cannot separate. The Milky Way band blends light from many stars. We first look from inside its disk, then outside, to see where the band comes from. Our galaxy has differently shaped neighbours. Comparing their selected sizes needs one length ruler.
narration.cue: Change from ground sky to the along-disk view; explore named-star distances, the whole Milky Way and common-scale galaxy comparisons.

narration.label: Inward to our home
narration.text: Locate the Sun in the galaxy and approach nearby stars, the Solar System, Earth and Moon, and finally Earth. A separate comparison window explores different stellar families. Some planets orbit one star, while others travel around two. A star may also have a black-hole companion. Planets reflect starlight; bright gas near a black hole is not light emitted by the black hole itself.
narration.cue: Approach Earth through the inward stops. Separately play Kepler-16 or Cygnus X-1, then return to Earth and Moon.

narration.label: Outward to the cosmos
narration.text: Look outward from the Milky Way. Our galaxy and many others belong to the Local Group. The nearby Virgo Cluster is another structure to compare. Associations across still wider regions rely on observations and models. The cosmic web is a large-scale distribution, not a glowing shell. As the scale grows, one locator may stand for an entire galaxy; a drawn point does not always mean one star.
narration.cue: Explore the galaxy, group, neighbouring cluster, supercluster, cosmic web and observable region, distinguishing members, neighbours and statistical illustrations.

narration.label: Earth to the universe
narration.text: Finally zoom continuously from Earth. At first we can see its outline; later we need a locator. The Solar System, Milky Way and larger structures enter the view as the length ruler changes. The final dashed reference describes our observing range, not a wall around the whole universe. It does not make Earth the centre of the universe.
narration.cue: Play the fourth chapter, pause or reverse it, and compare the physical ruler, location anchor and current model limits.
